judge_assessment.explanation: Both hard failures hold, and this is the most lopsided coverage case in my slice. Every one of the ten problems is split into (a)/(b)/(c) parts, and verify.json carries one entry per id except id 8, which has two. Problem 1 asks (a) name the base, exponent and result, (b) rewrite in logarithmic form, (c) what does log_5 125 equal — and id 1 is a single eval returning 3, covering (c) alone. Problem 3 prints a four-cell table of powers of 3 for the student to fill and then asks for the exponential statement and the log's value; id 3 is one eval returning 4, so the table is untouched. Problem 9 asks (a) convert to exponential form, (b) solve, (c) verify 2x-3 is positive AND say why the check is required, against a single `solve` returning [14]. The judge's blanket 'problems 1 through 10' is hedged with 'generally', which is fair: id 8 is the one well-covered problem, its two named outputs — the change-of-base quotient and the approximation — carried by an `equiv` and an `approx`. The second failure is exact: problem 4(c) 'say why the logarithm of a number between 0 and 1 comes out negative' and problem 9(c) 'say in one sentence why that check is required' have no manual entry and gate_chain_manual_flags is false. All ten terminal values recompute correctly, including log_3 20 = 2.727 and the doubling time 15.747. REJECT is correct.

strengths_to_preserve: The reference card is value-free by design and says so — 'No values are filled in --- use the numbers given in each problem' — with base, exponent and result each named on its own line. It gives the student the vocabulary the problems then demand without pre-solving anything.

The sheet covers the cases where conversion is not cosmetic rather than repeating the easy direction: a negative logarithm (problem 4), a fractional one (problem 6, log_8 2 = 1/3), a fractional exponent (problem 7, 4^(3/2)), a compound argument (problem 9, log_5(2x-3)), and a real growth model (problem 10).

Problem 5(b) — 'Between which two consecutive whole numbers must x lie? Say how you know from powers of 2' — anchors the decimal 5.322 to 2^5 = 32 < 40 < 64 = 2^6. A student who produces a wrong decimal has a way to notice.

Problem 8 derives the change-of-base formula rather than issuing it: start from log_3 x = y, convert, take natural logs of both sides, solve for y. And it is the one problem whose printed outputs are both verified, so it also shows the file's own best practice.

The directions make labelling a standing requirement — 'Before converting, label which given number is the base, which is the exponent, and which is the result' — which is the right habit for this topic even though it is currently the least verified thing on the sheet.

root_causes.description: Every problem is multi-part and the contract counts problems. Ten ids across roughly twenty-six printed response slots are discharged by eleven entries, all on terminal numbers. The failure is structural rather than careless: the author had no mechanism that would have complained.
evidence: SKILL.md:189 — 'verification hard-fails unless every problem id 1..N has at least one check (use `manual` for the unverifiable ones), so a partially-verified answer key can never slip through'. The trailing promise does not follow from the rule: the rule counts PROBLEMS, the promise is about ANSWERS.
scripts/verify.py:2020 — the coverage gate is `missing = [i for i in range(1, problem_count + 1) if i not in ids]`, i.e. membership of the id set, never a count of printed response slots

tests/check_layout.py:47-49 and ANSWER_RE at :99 — the layout gate requires that each item CONTAIN one answer-location macro; it never compares that count against the number of verify entries carrying the id
worksheet.tex: problems 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 each print three lettered parts; problems 3, 6, 8 print two
verify.json: exactly one entry per id except id 8, which has two — eleven entries for ten multi-part problems
worksheet.tex problem 3 prints a four-column tabular of powers of 3 with a blank 'value' row; id 3 is a single eval of log(81, 3)

root_causes.description: The conversion itself — the equivalence b^y = x <=> log_b x = y — is the entire subject of the task, and there is no entry type that expresses 'the student wrote the correct converted STATEMENT'. So the author records the number the statement evaluates to, which is a proxy that a student can produce without ever performing the conversion. A bare 3 does not witness 'log_5 125 = 3' having been written.
evidence: task_contract focus: 'converting between exponential and logarithmic forms'
verify.json ids 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 all use `eval` on the numeric result; none records the converted statement the stem asks for

worksheet.tex problem 1(b) 'Rewrite the statement in logarithmic form'; problem 2(b) 'Rewrite the statement in exponential form'; problem 6(a) 'Write the conversion: log_8 2 = y becomes what exponential statement?'

improvements.title: Every printed response slot needs its own verification entry, not one per problem
improvements.proposed_change: Require an entry per lettered part. In tests/check_layout.py, count \textbf{(a)}/(b)/(c) part markers inside each \problem segment and fail when the number of verify entries carrying that id is smaller. Most of the missing parts are already expressible: problem 3's table row is four evals (3^1..3^4), problem 5(b)'s bracketing is two evals (2**5 -> 32 and 2**6 -> 64), problem 7(c)'s check is an eval of log(8, 4) -> 3/2, problem 9(c)'s positivity check is an eval of 2*x-3 at 14 -> 25 > 0, and problem 10(a)'s doubled-value equation is an eval of 1200*1.045**t at the found t. Also fix SKILL.md:189 so the stated promise matches the rule.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture problem printing three \textbf{(a)}/(b)/(c) markers with a single verify entry for its id; assert check_layout.py exits non-zero reporting 3 parts against 1 entry. Today it exits 0.
improvements.expected_impact: This sheet has the widest gap in my slice — roughly twenty-six printed slots behind eleven entries. Part-counting is a cheap, unambiguous signal because the parts are explicitly marked up in the source, and it would have caught nine of the ten problems here.
improvements.risk: Low-medium for the counting itself, since the markers are literal \textbf{(a)} strings. The risk is that a part is genuinely open reasoning, in which case the required entry is `manual`, not a computational one — the gate must accept either.

improvements.title: The converted statement itself is never verified, only the number it evaluates to
improvements.proposed_change: Add an equivalence-of-statements check so a conversion can be verified as a conversion. The `equiv` type already compares two expressions; extend it (or add a sibling) to accept a pair of EQUATIONS and confirm they have the same solution set — {"type": "equiv_statement", "given": "5**3 = 125", "expected": "log(125, 5) = 3"}. Then problem 1(b), 2(b), 4(a), 6(a), 7(a), 9(a) and 10(b) each get an entry that witnesses the actual instructional target instead of its numeric shadow. Until that lands, an interim measure with today's schema: record the converted form's components as separate evals (base, exponent, result), which at least binds the labelling the directions demand.
improvements.regression_test: Add a verify.py unit test asserting equiv_statement('5**3 = 125', 'log(125, 5) = 3') passes and equiv_statement('5**3 = 125', 'log(5, 125) = 3') fails on the swapped base and argument — the exact error this worksheet exists to prevent. No such check exists today.
improvements.expected_impact: Moves verification onto the task's stated focus. Right now a student could write every conversion backwards and still produce all ten verified numbers, because the numbers were computed from the correct form by the author, not read off the student's.
improvements.risk: Medium. Equation-level equivalence needs care with domains (log_b x = y is defined only for x > 0, b > 0, b != 1) and a solution-set comparison can be expensive. Restrict version one to the log/exp pair pattern, which is the case that matters here.

improvements.title: Written explanations the worksheet demands are recorded as machine-verified rather than manual
improvements.proposed_change: Declare ids 4 and 9 manual for their (c) explanations, and add problem 5(b)'s 'Say how you know from powers of 2' — which the judge did not list — to the same treatment. Gate with the prose scan and merge SKILL.md:249 into :257.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture problem whose (c) part reads 'say in one sentence why that check is required' with only a solve entry for the id; assert check_layout.py exits non-zero. Silent today.
improvements.expected_impact: Three written explanations gain honest status, and the delivery message stops claiming 'Nothing is claimed as verified without a check behind it' on a sheet where most printed parts have no check behind them.
improvements.risk: Medium; keyword over-fire on directions and hint clauses. Scope to \problem segments, warn-only first.

improvements.title: final_response.md names the three deliverables but gives no filenames
improvements.proposed_change: As with curr-375, the response opens 'Three PDFs are ready: the student worksheet (6 pages), a step-by-step answer key, and a two-page skills summary' and never prints a filename, while eight of the ten cases in this slice do. Generate the closing list from build.sh's '── PDFs ──' block instead of describing it, and add a check to tests/check_artifact_health.py requiring each produced PDF basename to appear in final_response.md.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture final_response.md describing 'three PDFs' with no basenames against a build that produced them; assert check_artifact_health.py exits non-zero naming the missing files. No such check today.
improvements.expected_impact: Makes the deliverable locatable. Scored p2 rather than the canonical p1 because all three artifacts ARE named by role and only the filenames are absent.
improvements.risk: Low; the names are already printed by build.sh.

case_summary: Every terminal value is correct — I recomputed all ten, including log_8 2 = 1/3, log_3 20 = 2.7268 and the 15.747-year doubling time. The concept-model work is genuine: a value-free reference card naming base, exponent and result; a powers-of-3 table to read log_3 81 off; a bracketing step that pins 5.322 between 2^5 and 2^6; and a derivation rather than an issuance of change of base. The rejection is well founded and this is the widest coverage gap in my slice — ten multi-part problems presenting roughly twenty-six printed responses, against eleven verify entries that are almost all terminal numbers. Two things compound it. The lettered parts are explicitly marked in the source, so a part counter would have caught nine of ten problems trivially. And more fundamentally, there is no way in the schema to verify a CONVERTED STATEMENT, which is the task's entire focus, so the author recorded the number the statement evaluates to — a proxy a student can satisfy while writing the conversion backwards. Problem 8 shows the file's own better standard, carrying both of its named outputs. Separately, final_response.md gives no filenames.
